1:
Chrysostom opens by complaining that many do not know the book exists, and urges that it may profit us no less than the Gospels, since here the predictions uttered there are seen coming to pass and the change the Spirit worked in the disciples can be watched happening. Its title was never fixed. Robertson sets out the manuscript readings, from the bare word for acts to the long form with holy attached, and judges the received title certainly wrong; Clarke collects the names it has borne, the transactions of the apostles in one codex, a fifth Gospel to some, the Gospel of the Holy Spirit to one Greek writer and the demonstration of the resurrection to another; Barnes adds that the word means doings and not decrees, and observes that what the book actually records is largely the doings of two men. On the opening phrase Ellicott notes that the noun means a discourse and was used so by Xenophon of the books of a history, and that the adjective is strictly first rather than former; Robertson agrees that a superlative used of two implies no lost third volume. Gill and Wesley both mark where the join falls, at the ascension.

Henry pauses over the dedication, since the Gospel called the man most excellent and this book calls him only Theophilus, and offers three guesses: that he had left the office the title belonged to, that he had grown old enough to think less of such forms, or that Luke now knew him well enough to drop them. Ellicott allows the inference and calls it precarious. On the proofs of the resurrection Clarke enumerates seven: appearances to different persons at different times, the eating and drinking, the appointment kept in Galilee, the body offered to be handled, the teaching, the showing to more than five hundred at once, and the continuing of it for forty days. Ellicott observes that the Greek has no word answering to infallible but that the noun was a technical term of the rhetoricians for proofs carrying certainty as against those merely probable, and Calvin says the same from Aristotle, that this word names what is necessary in a sign. Calvin adds why it matters: without the resurrection the gospel falls flat and no faith remains, its whole authority resting on our knowing that a living Christ speaks to us. Lightfoot turns the forty days against a slander using the same number, since the man so accused gave sufficient testimony to his own innocence by conversing among men for forty days after death.

The word for the last gathering is disputed. Some versions render it eating together, which Gill reports and Clarke traces to a variant, while Barnes says the Greek will not bear that sense and Ellicott calls the etymology mistaken; Lightfoot settles it by derivation, taking the word not from salt but from the noun for an assembly, and citing the historians for that use. Robertson concedes only that salt was the mark of hospitality and that Jesus did on occasion eat with them. Lightfoot adds what nobody else does, that after the resurrection he never appeared among them except by surprise, save at the meeting in Galilee he had appointed. On the two baptisms Cyril presses the comparison as far as it will go: the grace was not partial but complete, for as the man plunged in water is encompassed on every side so were they wholly baptized — except that water washes only the outside while the Spirit baptizes the soul within, as fire passing into iron makes the whole of it fire, so that what was cold burns and what was black shines. Clarke draws the opposite lesson from the verse, that baptism cannot always mean plunging; and Wesley extends the promise past the apostles to all believers, reserving the extraordinary gifts.
6:
Three of them notice the question was put by a deputation. Chrysostom says they came together so that weight of numbers might shame him into answering, having understood that his earlier refusal about the day was a refusal and not ignorance; they would not have asked again had they been satisfied. Henry has them coming in a body and putting it as the sense of the house; Wesley thinks the design was concerted beforehand. He adds the motive: having heard the Spirit was coming they thought themselves fit to be told, and were ready enough for freedom, having no appetite for further danger and wanting only to breathe again. Calvin is harshest, calling it marvellous rudeness that after three years of teaching they should betray as much ignorance as if they had heard nothing, and counting as many errors as words — an earthly kingdom, a present date for it, a triumph demanded before the battle and wages before the work, the whole confined to the Israel of the flesh. Barnes explains the persistence historically, the death having checked the expectation and the resurrection revived it, so that they now wanted the Romans thrust out. Where they stood is itself disputed: Barnes puts the scene on Olivet, Clarke and Lightfoot on a mountain in Galilee.

On the two words for time they agree on the distinction and differ on how hard to press it. Clarke makes the first any large stretch, an era, an olympiad, a year, and the second the particular opportunity within it; Wesley reduces that to a longer and a shorter space; Barnes has one indefinite and the other fixed; Ellicott notes the pair is characteristic of Luke and Paul, and that the answer touches the season rather than the nature of what they hoped for. Robertson doubts it always holds, and turns the verse on the reader, remarking how eager people have always been to fix dates for the second coming, as the apostles were about their political kingdom, and calling the reservation a gentle hint about the limits of curiosity. Cyril gives the warning both edges: no one should be curious about the time nor venture to declare it, and equally no one should slumber, the hour being unlooked for. Calvin makes it a rule of learning, to go as far forward as our Master goes in teaching and be willing to be ignorant of what he conceals. Clarke alone turns the clause into an argument about God himself, that having all in his own power he is no necessary agent and frames no decree he must be compelled to execute.

Clarke and Ellicott both object that the English uses one word for two Greek ones, the first meaning authority and liberty of action, the second the energy communicated, often put for a miracle outright. Robertson sharpens it: the power promised is not the power they had in mind, with its organisation and equipment on the Roman model, and their question was itself the proof they needed another kind; he adds that the word for witnesses is the one our martyrs comes from. Ellicott finds the whole book laid out in the clause that follows, Jerusalem, Judaea, Samaria and the ends of the earth answering to its great divisions, and calls the sentence its key-note. Calvin traces the fault to its root, that curiosity rises almost always from idleness or distrust, the one cured by meditating on the promises and the other by attending to the commandment; and he charges them with catching at gifts proper to the Spirit before receiving him, and with wanting their ease in the inn when called out to war. Gill puts the correction plainly: instead of the ease and wealth they looked for they must expect labour and affliction; and Wesley says they were to witness by suffering as much as by preaching.
9:
Barnes and Calvin give the same argument for why the departure was staged as it was. Had he vanished secretly, or at night, the disciples would have been left amazed and doubting what had become of him; instead it happened in open day, from an elevated place open on every side, while they were in conversation with him and looking directly at him, so that the man they saw go was unmistakably the man they had been talking to. Clarke uses the same circumstances against a rationalising account he despises, which makes the taking up a walk into some cloud-capped mountain and the two figures a pair of priests, remarking that such an opinion has nevertheless been espoused by men of considerable learning. Ellicott raises the opposite difficulty, that the Gospels say remarkably little about an event so prominent in the creeds, two of them not recording it at all; and he answers it neatly, that the very reason for their reticence is that the fact was already creed and had been taught to every catechumen, so that they had no motive to embellish it as later legends embellished other things. Leo looks back over the interval, saying the forty days were given to instruction because death had so disturbed the disciples that a torpor of distrust crept over them, the women's report having sounded like raving.

The gazing is described rather than explained. Barnes gives the compound of feeling in it, amazement and disappointment and curiosity with the wish to catch a last glimpse; Robertson notes the tense and puts it that they saw him slipping from their eyes as the cloud bore him away. On the two figures Ellicott prefers were standing, since the appearance was sudden and the approach unnoticed, and compares them to the forms at the empty tomb, in white like the young priests of the Temple. Clarke calls them angels in human shape and reads the white as purity and glory. Calvin will not argue about whether the bodies were real, saying only that whatever they were they were certainly not men, and takes the clothing as a mark of dignity given so that the disciples should listen the more attentively and so that we should know the vision came from God. Gill sets it down more simply, that after the cloud took him they went on looking upward in case they should see him again.

Whether the address carries a rebuke divides them. Gill says it was not thrown at their country but served to show the speakers knew them, and to mark the grace that chose such mean persons. Barnes finds no reproach in the name but a slight censure in the question, and lists the possible impropriety: disappointment that the kingdom was not restored, an expectation that he would soon reappear, or too much attachment to a bodily presence better bestowed in heaven. Calvin rejects the opprobrious reading outright and thinks the naming was meant to fix their attention, since strangers addressed them as though they knew them perfectly; and he defends the gazing itself, asking where they should look for Christ if not heavenward, before answering that they were reproved not for looking up but for wanting to see him with their eyes and for hoping he would come straight back. On the promise of return Robertson notes that the personal name is the assurance, and that the emphatic doubling covers the manner as well as the fact. Clarke and Ellicott both report the old opinion that the appearance will be on the mount he left from, Ellicott tracing it to the prophet who set the judgment in the valley below and the Judge's feet on the hill, and Clarke adding that some refer the angels' words instead to the coming destruction of the nation.
12:
The measure of the distance is made to carry a surprising amount. Chrysostom infers the day of the week from it, since the distance would not have been given that way unless they were then walking a sabbath's allowance. Ellicott takes it further and builds a chronology on it, that the forty days had already expired and this last meeting fell on the following sabbath, eight days before Pentecost, finding a fitness in the Lord entering his rest on the day of rest. Robertson refuses the whole inference, pointing out that Luke says only that the mount is that far from the city and not that Jesus was at that distance when he went. Lightfoot supplies the rule behind the phrase, that going beyond the city bounds on the sabbath was punished, that some reckoned the bounds by the compass of the Israelites' camp, and that the scribes fixed them at two thousand cubits; Barnes and Wesley both give that figure and note that Moses had determined nothing about it. Clarke meets the geographical difficulty instead, since the mount is nearer the city than Bethany is, and solves it by making the ascent happen where the two districts touch. Henry adds why the place was fitting, that where the sufferings began the reproach of them was rolled away.

Where they lodged afterwards divides them squarely. Gill runs through the houses that have been proposed — the evangelist's, the mother of John Mark's, the leper's, which he rules out as being in Bethany, and those of Nicodemus and Joseph — and concludes it was no private house at all but the temple. Clarke leans the same way, since the Gospel says they were continually in the temple, while granting that private upper rooms were used for reading the law. Barnes says there is no evidence for the temple and that it is not very probable; Robertson says flatly it was a private house, and takes the word continually to mean on proper occasions. Ellicott works from the vocabulary, noting the article and distinguishing this room from the one where the Passover was eaten, that being a guest-chamber on the first floor for meals and this a loft above it used for retirement and prayer. Calvin reads the same word socially: the upper part of a house was what landlords let to tenants, keeping the better rooms themselves, so the company was crowded into a narrow space and stayed there rather than separate before the Spirit came.

Calvin takes the list of names as an occasion for two arguments. He denies that Peter's standing first proves any supremacy, observing that on such reasoning the mother of Christ would be inferior to all the other women, since she is named last of them; and he prefers to render the next word wives rather than women, on the ground that the apostles afterwards travelled with their wives, so that they are unlikely to have been separated now, and there was no reason to shut them out of what was about to come. Ellicott keeps the wider sense and thinks these women were among the writer's own informants, naming those the Gospel had named and remarking that here we lose sight of them and everything after is conjecture; Gill identifies them simply as those who came up from Galilee. On the last clause Clarke reports that many copies omit the words for supplication and that Griesbach struck them out, then refuses the argument that they are redundant, since prayer asks while supplication expostulates and urges the petition again; Barnes had called the two nearly synonymous. Robertson gives the adverb its force, one mind and one spirit, and says they stuck to the praying until the answer came, while Wesley notes that the brethren named here had not believed until near the end.
15:
The company numbered a hundred and twenty, and Clarke thinks the figure deliberate, that being the number the Jews required to constitute a council in a city, so that what met here was a complete court before which the election could properly be held. Robertson will have none of it, calling the number simply how many were there and a crowd for such a room. Ellicott guesses who they were, the seventy perhaps, with Joseph and Nicodemus and some of the five hundred, and thinks the word for names hints at a list the writer worked from. Why Peter should speak first is answered without much difference: Gill and Barnes make him the senior and most forward, Gill adding that a man who had lately denied his master would be eager to show his zeal; Ellicott hears in the tone of the speech a man who knew himself forgiven and restored, for whom doing the work faithfully was a better fruit of repentance than any public confession. Calvin turns the same fact against a conclusion drawn from it, that because Peter speaks in the assembly he must be head of the church — as though no one might speak among the godly without becoming Pope. Henry and Calvin both explain why the gap had to be filled, the twelve answering to the twelve tribes, so that eleven teachers would have set everyone asking what became of the twelfth.

That the account of Judas is the historian's insertion is argued most fully by Gill, on four grounds: the disciples needed no telling of what all Jerusalem knew; Jerusalem would not be spoken of that way by a man standing in it; there was no sense in explaining a word of their own language in a language they did not use; and a name could hardly have become current in six weeks. Calvin agrees and dismisses the reply that Peter was addressing Galileans of a different speech as vain and frivolous, since the difference was one of pronunciation. How he died is less settled. Barnes has him hang himself and then fall and burst; Wesley supposes the rope broke at or just before death; Robertson observes that the word means flat on the face rather than headlong. Lightfoot proposes what none of the others contemplate, that the devil caught him into the air as soon as the money was flung back, strangled him and dashed him on the ground; and he questions whether the Greek need mean that Judas hanged himself rather than that he was hanged. Robertson reports two explanations of the field's name, the price of blood and the blood spilt there, and says both may stand.

On the citation Barnes notes it follows neither the Hebrew nor the Greek exactly, the plural being turned singular and a clause about tents dropped. Ellicott states the purpose rather than the mechanics: they were not to be staggered by the treachery or the apparent collapse of their hopes, since the Psalms had already shown the righteous sufferer betrayed and the betrayer requited, so nothing strange had happened; and he declines to enter on either the original occasion of those Psalms or the difficulty of their curses, neither being within the horizon of the speaker's thought. Robertson makes the same point about the speaker's position, that the Spirit had not yet come and the necessity urged is logical rather than moral. The last word draws a protest. Clarke objects that rendering it bishopric is improper, the charge of Judas being nothing like a diocese with its estate and emoluments, and traces the Greek through the Saxon to the English word, its sense being simply an overseer; Robertson objects more briefly, that the ecclesiastical meaning came later and what is meant is over-seership. Wesley cuts it shortest of all, glossing the word as his apostleship.
21:
Ellicott states the qualification as symbolism and evidence together: the Twelve had to appear complete, answering to the tribes, and the man filling the gap had to testify from his own knowledge of the ministry and above all of the resurrection, a condition even by Paul's reckoning. Robertson draws the consequence nobody else states, that a qualification of that kind must very soon exhaust the supply of men who can meet it. Gill reads the phrase as excluding women from the office; Barnes thinks the seventy are chiefly in view. Clarke protests at the English of the next verse, there being no word for ordained in the Greek at all, and prefers an older printed version that renders the two verses without it. Calvin anticipates an objection, that a psalm about transferring an office does not by itself oblige anyone to hold an election; and answers that having been charged with ordering the church they had only to learn the Lord's will and act on it, since when God means to use us we must not linger once we know what he wants.

Why two were put forward rather than one exercises Calvin most. He canvasses the possibilities and rejects them: that the men were indistinguishable, which would be no reason to resort to a lot; that one was plainly the more esteemed; or that the company was divided in affection, which he refuses to believe of an assembly just praised for its unity. Ellicott leaves open whether the two were put up by the apostles for the whole body to choose between, or by the body for settlement by lot; Clarke thinks the disciples were genuinely divided and so referred it upward; Wesley marks the exact point of transfer, that consultation could carry them so far and no further, and that the lot properly begins where no ordinary method will decide. On the prayer they divide over who is addressed. Barnes assembles reasons for holding it was made to the Lord Jesus, from the title used and the heart-searching claimed elsewhere for him; Ellicott raises the same question and inclines the other way, on the analogy of a later prayer to the Father to work through the Son, while granting that Stephen's dying words show prayer to the Son was familiar. Robertson notes what the petition assumes, that the choice is already made and only needs disclosing.

The phrase about his own place is read almost unanimously of Judas and against him. Lightfoot supplies the idiom from the rabbis, where Balaam went to his own place meaning hell, and the friends of Job are said to come each from his own place, glossed as the place cut out for him there. Robertson calls the words a picture worthy of Dante and says the man made ready his own berth and went to it; Wesley has him going to what his crimes deserved and he had chosen, far from the others and in the region of death. Ellicott alone notes that the grammar is ambiguous and that some have referred the phrase to the man about to be chosen, taking up his own place among the Twelve, though he thinks the other connection more natural; Clarke adds a variant that would read just or proper place instead. On the lot Barnes argues in three steps that voting is not meant, from the word, from the expression about the lot falling, and from Jewish practice; Ellicott agrees and describes the urn shaken until one tablet came out, Gill the balloting and counting. Robertson observes that to a Jew the lot suggested not gambling but the old way of learning God's will, and Calvin defends the practice against those who condemn it outright, granting that divination by lots is devilish while dividing an inheritance by them is lawful.
